overview.text: A website is an organized set of linked web pages and related resources, usually grouped under one domain name. It is different from a single web page, which is a browser-displayable document, and from a web server, the computer that hosts websites. Pages have web addresses called URLs, and links let people move between resources. A browser requests those resources from servers and displays the returned content, which may include text, images, styles, or scripts. Websites are one way people use the World Wide Web’s system of identified, connected resources. The Web was proposed at CERN in 1989 to help scientists share information; CERN’s public release of the software in 1993 helped it spread.

key_facts.text: A web page is a browser-displayable document; a website groups linked pages and associated resources, usually under a shared domain.
A URL is a web address used to locate a resource; hyperlinks connect resources and let users navigate between them.
A browser retrieves and displays web resources; a web server hosts them. A search engine helps users find pages but is not the browser.
Some websites are single-page apps: they update content within one page, and the address may not change as users navigate.
The Web was conceived at CERN to support information-sharing among scientists. CERN put its software in the public domain on April 30, 1993.
